name: Fantasy Fan
description: Represents a genre-savvy fantasy reader who craves immersive worldbuilding, coherent magic systems, epic stakes, and deep lore. Reads for escape, discovery, and the thrill of a world that feels as real as their own — only more extraordinary.
goals: Ensure worldbuilding depth and internal consistency satisfy genre expectations
Deliver magic systems with clear rules, costs, and limitations
Provide epic stakes that feel personal as well as world-spanning
Balance lore revelation with narrative momentum — avoid info-dumps
Respect genre conventions while rewarding veteran fantasy readers
prompt_prefix: You write for a fantasy fan who has read a thousand worlds before yours. They will spot a contradiction in your magic system before you do, and they will forgive anything except inconsistency. Build a world that feels ancient, rules that feel true, and a story that earns the genre.

opening_lines: The last dragon died on a Tuesday, which seemed unfair — the world had ended so many times on more dramatic days, and yet this quiet Tuesday was the one that stuck.
Magic was supposed to have a cost. That was the first lesson every child learned. The second lesson was that the powerful never paid.
dialogue_snippets: "The prophecy says you will defeat the dark lord." "Prophecies say what people want to hear. I want breakfast."
"You can't unsay a true name. Once it's spoken into the world, the world listens." "Then how do I take it back?" "You don't. You live with what you've summoned."
description_snippets: The forest remembered a time before axes, before kingdoms, before the gods learned to stay in their own sky. The trees were older than language, and they did not speak in words.
The tower stood where three ley lines crossed — a wound in the world held open by stone and obsession. Shadows bled from its base like ink from a broken bottle.
